prompt.context: You are the manager of a food concessions operation at a stadium. You have 100 employees who can each sell ONLY ONE of the two products you offer: Coke or Sprite. Having done careful market-demand studies, you know with a VERY high degree of certainty that the salespeople you assign will create daily revenues according to the following schedule: The first person you assign to sell Coke will produce revenues of $100, the second $99, the third $98, and so forth. The first person you assign to sell Sprite will produce revenues of $90, the second $88, the third $86, and so forth.
prompt.question: How many people do you allocate to sell each soft drink to maximize expected daily revenues?

framework: Recognize diminishing marginal returns: each additional salesperson added to a product generates less revenue than the previous one
Build a two-column table listing marginal revenue for each additional employee by product (Coke: $100, $99, $98…; Sprite: $90, $88, $86…)
Greedily assign each of the 100 employees to whichever product offers the highest next marginal revenue
Identify the repeating pattern once Sprite's marginal revenue enters the range of Coke's marginal revenues
Apply the pattern to count total assignments without enumerating all 100 rows

questions.prompt: Walk through the allocation logic step by step. How do you determine who gets assigned to which product?
questions.guidance: A strong answer builds the two-column marginal-revenue table (Coke decreases by $1 per person; Sprite decreases by $2 per person). The candidate compares marginal revenues sequentially: assign to whichever product has the higher next marginal revenue. First 10 employees all go to Coke (Coke marginal revenues 100–91 are all above Sprite's first marginal revenue of $90). At employee 11, Coke's next marginal is $90 and Sprite's is also $90 — tie, but Sprite enters the competition. Then Coke resumes ($89, $88) while Sprite's next is $88 — yielding a 2-Coke-then-1-Sprite repeating pattern among the remaining 90 employees.

math.setup: Coke marginal revenue for nth person = 101 − n. Sprite marginal revenue for nth person = 92 − 2n. After the first 10 go to Coke, 90 employees remain. Among these, every 3rd employee goes to Sprite (pattern: Coke, Coke, Sprite repeating).
steps: Employees 1–10: all assigned to Coke (Coke MR = $100 down to $91, all above Sprite's $90 first MR)
Employee 11: Sprite ($90) ties Coke's next MR ($90) — assign to Sprite
Employees 12–13: Coke ($89, $88) both exceed Sprite's next MR ($88 ties at employee 13, but Coke had $89 first)
Pattern established: among remaining 90 employees, 1 out of every 3 goes to Sprite
math.answer: 70 employees sell Coke, 30 employees sell Sprite

recommendation: Assign 70 employees to sell Coke and 30 employees to sell Sprite
This allocation equates the marginal revenue of the last employee assigned to each product, maximizing total daily revenues
risks: Actual demand may deviate from the demand schedule if stadium attendance varies
Employees may not be perfectly interchangeable in selling ability
next_steps: Monitor actual daily revenues per product and adjust allocation if demand schedules shift
Consider dynamic reallocation during the event if early sales data differs from projections
